differences.title: 1. DATA MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Grafana is a visualization layer: it queries many backends (Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch, Tempo) via data source plugins. Your telemetry storage and semantics are defined by those systems, not Grafana itself.
differences.rightDesc: Datadog is a unified platform: metrics, logs, and traces are normalized into Datadog’s internal model. Agents forward events, enrich with tags, and store into Datadog-managed pipelines for consistent correlation across signals.

differences.title: 2. INGESTION PATH
differences.leftDesc: Grafana typically reads at dashboard query time. If you federate data, it happens in the upstream systems (Prometheus federation, Loki sharding). Grafana schedules queries and renders results without owning ingestion.
differences.rightDesc: Datadog uses the Datadog Agent (and language tracers) to ship telemetry continuously. The hosted intake applies parsing, sampling, rate controls, and rollups before indexing—reducing query-time work for the user.

differences.title: 3. SCALING & STORAGE
differences.leftDesc: Grafana scales horizontally as a stateless frontend, but long-term retention and indexing depend on each data source you operate. High-cardinality risk sits in Prometheus/Loki/etc., requiring tuning per engine.
differences.rightDesc: Datadog abstracts storage and retention behind its managed service. You configure retention, sampling, and aggregation policies; Datadog handles indexing, shards, and performance characteristics centrally for all tenants.

differences.title: 4. TRACING EXPERIENCE
differences.leftDesc: Grafana supports distributed tracing by connecting to backends like Grafana Tempo or Jaeger. Trace-to-log/trace-to-metric linking depends on shared identifiers and exemplars supported by your chosen trace system.
differences.rightDesc: Datadog provides trace-native ingestion and UI. It correlates spans with metrics and logs using consistent trace IDs and service/resource tagging conventions, offering faster cross-navigation without hand-wiring exemplars across systems.

differences.title: 5. ALERTING MECHANICS
differences.leftDesc: Grafana alerting evaluates expressions against a data source on a schedule (or via its rule engine). Alert state, grouping, and notification routing depend on the metrics/log query outputs and Grafana rule configuration.
differences.rightDesc: Datadog alerting is tightly integrated with its monitoring and SLO tooling. Thresholds, anomaly detection, and composite monitors are computed over Datadog-managed streams, enabling consistent behavior across teams and sources.

differences.title: 6. CARDINALITY & COST CONTROL
differences.leftDesc: Grafana can display high-cardinality data, but cost/performance constraints come from each underlying engine. For Prometheus or Loki, you must manage label design, sampling, and retention strategies independently.
differences.rightDesc: Datadog offers centralized governance knobs like sampling, metric limits, cardinality controls, and ingestion filters. Because it owns the intake pipeline, it can enforce guardrails before data becomes expensive to store and query.

differences.title: 7. DEPLOYMENT MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Grafana can run fully on-prem or in Kubernetes with your observability stack. This offers control over network egress, data residency, and integrations, but you must operate each component for reliability and upgrades.
differences.rightDesc: Datadog is SaaS-first with agent-based collection, minimizing operational overhead. You trade some infrastructure control for faster onboarding and consistent upgrades, while Datadog manages ingestion, indexing, and query performance.
